Feebler
FEE-bler
adj., comparative. (weaker; more lacking in strength)
Comparative of feeble, from Old French feble, from Latin flebilis, lamentable, from flere, to weep; a word for weakness rooted in a word for grief.

Biblical Definition

But when the cattle were feeble, he put them not in: so the feebler were Laban's, and the stronger Jacob's.

The verse closes Jacob's long, uneasy contract with Laban, fourteen years of service turned into a breeding strategy that left Jacob prospering and Laban's flocks visibly diminished. On its surface it describes animal husbandry; underneath it, the text has already told us what Jacob did not fully disclose to Laban, that his success came by cunning as much as by the LORD's blessing he later claims in Genesis 31. Feebler here marks the visible outcome of an arrangement weighted, by craft or by providence or both, toward one party's increase and the other's loss. Jacob's own account to his wives afterward insists the LORD hath taken away the cattle of your father, and given them to me, folding what looks like clever breeding into divine providence. The text leaves both readings available, Jacob's partial deceit and the LORD's overruling hand, without collapsing one into the other; Scripture is comfortable narrating a man's craftiness and God's providence operating in the same event without excusing the former by the latter. The feebler and the stronger divide, two flocks under one sky, becomes an early picture of how the LORD's purposes can ride on top of, without ever sanctifying, a man's own schemes.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828), from FEEBLE: comparative degree; weaker; wanting strength in a greater degree than another.

expand to see more

FEEBLE, a. Weak; infirm; wanting strength or vigor.

FEEBLER is its comparative: weaker than another.

Genesis 30: the feebler cattle were Laban's, the stronger Jacob's.

Marks the visible result of Jacob's long contract with Laban.

Narrated alongside Jacob's own later claim of the LORD's providence in the matter.

Key Scripture

Gen 30:42 — "But when the cattle were feeble, he put them not in: so the feebler were Laban's, and the stronger Jacob's."

Modern Corruption

No live postmodern redefinition attaches; the recoverable principle is Scripture's refusal to let providence excuse craftiness.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. Feebler has simply become an uncommon word, replaced by weaker in ordinary speech.

The principle in the narrative is still instructive: the LORD's blessing on Jacob's increase did not require, and does not retroactively sanctify, every method by which Jacob pursued it. A modern believer tempted to read providential success as proof that the means used to get it were therefore godly should read Genesis 30 and 31 together, and note how carefully the text keeps the two apart.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

From Latin flebilis, lamentable, through Old French feble, feeble names a weakness the comparative -er measures against a stronger counterpart.

expand to see more

Flebilis, Latin for lamentable, lies behind feeble through Old French feble.

Feeble names a want of strength; feebler, its comparative degree.

Genesis 30 divides Laban's flocks and Jacob's by exactly this measure.

Jacob's own later words credit the LORD's providence for the increase.

The text narrates craft and providence together without equating them.

Usage

"the feebler were Laban's, and the stronger Jacob's — the outcome of a long contract"

"set beside Jacob's own later claim of the LORD's providence"

"an early picture of providence operating above, not sanctifying, human craft"
